subject: maths
stem:
Ira writes four claims about the number list 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, …

Which claim treats the list as a mathematical pattern?

options.A: The list looks neat, so it is a pattern even with no rule stated.
options.B: Explaining the list is what creates the even numbers in the first place.
options.C: Each term is 2 more than the one before, because we keep adding 2.
options.D: The same list also proves a new theorem about all infinite sequences.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Anya studies the whole-number list 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, …

Which claim correctly continues the list using its generative rule?

options.A: The next term is 10, because the list of whole numbers always grows by 1.
options.B: Writing the next odd number is what creates the odd numbers in the first place.
options.C: The next term is 11, because each term is 2 more than the one before.
options.D: The next term needs a closed formula for triangular numbers before it can be named.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Rina studies the three pictures in the figure. Each picture is a square grid of dots: a 1-by-1 square, then a 2-by-2 square, then a 3-by-3 square.

Which claim correctly describes how to draw the next picture?

options.A: Any larger cluster of dots works, without keeping the square-grid construction from picture to picture.
options.B: Drawing the next square grid is what creates the square numbers in the first place.
options.C: The next picture is a 4-by-4 square of 16 dots, because each picture is an n-by-n square for n = 1, 2, 3, …
options.D: The next picture needs the full chapter shape-sequence table before it can be drawn.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Isha builds an $n$-by-$n$ square of unit tiles. She peels it into $n$ nested L-shaped layers: the outermost L uses $2n-1$ tiles, then $2n-3$, and so on down to $1$.

Why does the sum of the first $n$ odd numbers equal $n^{2}$?

options.A: Any collection of odd numbers sums to a square, even if the odds are not the first $n$ consecutive odds starting at $1$.
options.B: The same L-layer story also explains the up-and-down sum of ordinary counting numbers, so that sum must equal $n^{2}$ too.
options.C: The $n$-by-$n$ square can be partitioned into those $n$ nested odd L-layers, so $1+3+\cdots+(2n-1)=n^{2}$.
options.D: The answer is "odd numbers", because that phrase is printed most often in the problem.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Anya writes the up-and-down sum $1+2+\cdots+n+\cdots+2+1$ with consecutive counting numbers that climb from $1$ to $n$ and then fall back to $1$.

Why does that sum equal $n^{2}$?

options.A: The sum equals $n^{2}$ for any climb-and-fall of whole numbers, even if the steps are not the consecutive counting numbers from $1$ to $n$ and back.
options.B: Say that $n^{2}$ is what produces the up-and-down counting sum, instead of arranging the sum to fill an $n$-by-$n$ square.
options.C: The climb from $1$ to $n$ and the fall back to $1$ can be paired to fill an $n$-by-$n$ square of unit tiles, so the sum is $n^{2}$.
options.D: The same story also forces triangular and hexagonal number identities, so those must equal $n^{2}$ too.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Rina builds a row of squares with matchsticks. Shape $1$ uses $4$ sticks, shape $2$ uses $7$ sticks, and shape $3$ uses $10$ sticks.

Which countable feature produces the related number sequence $4$, $7$, $10$, $\ldots$?

options.A: Count sticks on shape $1$ only, then reuse that same count for every later shape.
options.B: Count every interior angle in any polygon from the chapter, as if that also made this sequence.
options.C: Count the matchsticks in each whole shape; repeating that same count gives $4$, $7$, $10$, $\ldots$.
options.D: Pick the printed numeral $10$ alone because it is the largest number shown.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Omkar makes a tiny pencil mark on his notebook page and labels it P.

In geometry, what does this mark stand for?

options.A: A point: a precise location with no length, breadth, or thickness, named by the letter P.
options.B: A short line segment that starts at P and has a measurable length.
options.C: The black disk of graphite itself, which has a real size on the page.
options.D: Any decorative blot on the page, even when it does not name a location.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit draws a straight path that starts at point A, ends at point B, and does not continue past either point.

What has he drawn?

options.A: A line, because it is straight.
options.B: A ray starting at A and passing through B without ending.
options.C: A line segment AB, because it has two endpoints A and B.
options.D: A line segment even if he erases endpoint B and lets the path run on.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Esha marks three distinct points P, Q, and R on her paper that do not lie on one straight path.

How many distinct lines are determined by these points?

options.A: One line, because any set of points always lies on a single line.
options.B: Infinitely many lines, because one point alone already fixes infinitely many lines.
options.C: Three lines: PQ, QR, and RP, because each pair of distinct points determines exactly one line.
options.D: Nine lines, by multiplying three points by three possible directions.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Dev draws the ray shown in the figure. It starts at point A and passes through points B and C in that order.

Which label correctly names the ray?

options.A: Ray BA, because B and A both lie on the path.
options.B: Point A is produced by the ray, so any letter order is fine.
options.C: Ray AB or ray AC, because the starting point A comes first, then a point on the path.
options.D: Line ABC, treating the figure as a two-way line with no starting point.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Veena draws two rays from a common point O on her slate: ray OA and ray OB.

Which statement correctly describes the angle they form?

options.A: The vertex of the angle is arm OA.
options.B: OA and OB form this angle even if they start at two different points.
options.C: The rays share starting point O (the vertex); the arms are OA and OB; the angle may be named ∠AOB.
options.D: The angle is named ∠O because O is the first letter printed on the slate.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tara compares the two angles in the figure. Angle P has short arms and a wide turn. Angle Q has long arms and a narrow turn.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Angle Q is larger, because its arms are drawn longer.
options.B: The drawn arm lengths are what produce the amount of turn.
options.C: Angle P is larger, because it has the greater amount of turn about the vertex.
options.D: Compare decorative arrowheads on the rays before measuring the turn.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Mona has two card angles. She wants to know which is larger by overlaying them.

Which method decides correctly?

options.A: Lay them so the vertices miss each other, and still claim the overlay compares the angles.
options.B: Say that the larger angle is what produces a successful overlay, instead of using overlay to compare.
options.C: Place both vertices together and match one arm; the angle whose other arm lies outside is larger (they match if equal).
options.D: Use the same overlay test to decide which decorative colour on the card is brighter.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit looks at the figure: line AOB is straight through O, and ray OC meets AOB so that angle $1$ equals angle $2$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Angle $1$ is a right angle for any split of AOB, even when angle $1$ is not half of the straight angle.
options.B: He should first study the decorative history of the diagram before classifying any angle.
options.C: AOB is a straight angle (a half turn); because angle $1$ equals angle $2$, each is a right angle, so OC is perpendicular to AOB.
options.D: The answer is "straight angle", because those words are printed beside AOB, without using the equal split.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Esha measures an angle of $120^\circ$.

Which claim about its type is correct?

options.A: Call it acute even though $120^\circ$ is not less than $90^\circ$.
options.B: First study the decorative history of angle names before classifying $120^\circ$.
options.C: It is obtuse, because $90^\circ < 120^\circ < 180^\circ$.
options.D: It is "$120$", because that numeral is printed largest, without using the size classes.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Dev asks how a numerical degree measure is assigned to an angle formed by two rays from a point.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Answer "one-degree unit", naming that phrase instead of saying how many such units lie between the arms.
options.B: Count any collection of parts of a turn as degrees, even when those parts are not equal parts of a full turn.
options.C: A full turn is split into $360$ equal one-degree parts; the angle's measure is how many of those equal parts lie between its arms.
options.D: Say that the degree reading is what creates the equal one-degree parts, instead of counting those parts between the arms.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Veena must measure $\angle PQR$ with a protractor.

Which plan measures the angle correctly?

options.A: Place the protractor on ray $PQ$ and read a scale mark, without putting the center on vertex $Q$.
options.B: Say that reading a degree number is what creates $\angle PQR$, instead of aligning the protractor to the arms.
options.C: Place the center on $Q$, align one arm with the zero-degree line, and read the scale reached by the other arm.
options.D: After reading $\angle PQR$, treat that same reading as also fixing every other unmarked angle at $Q$, beyond measuring these two arms.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tara must construct a $65^\circ$ angle with ruler and protractor.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Call the finished drawing protractor angle only, without placing the protractor and marking $65^\circ$.
options.B: Place the protractor center on the vertex but skip aligning the base arm with the zero mark before reading $65^\circ$.
options.C: Choose a vertex and one base arm, seat the protractor center on the vertex, align the base arm with $0^\circ$, mark $65^\circ$ on the correct scale, and draw the second arm through that mark.
options.D: Mark $65$ only because that number is printed in the stem, without using the protractor steps.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qadir stands in a height line with other children. The rule is: each child says the count of taller children standing immediately next to that child. Qadir says "1".

What does Qadir's "1" report?

options.A: The count of taller children standing immediately next to him.
options.B: His own height in centimetres.
options.C: The total number of children in the whole line.
options.D: How many children in the line are shorter than him.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Parul writes this number grid (neighbours are left, right, top, and bottom only):

4  7  3
6  9  5
2  8  1

A supercell is greater than every immediate neighbour.

Which cell is a supercell?

options.A: The cell with 9
options.B: The cell with 8
options.C: The cell with 7
options.D: The cell with 6

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Indira fills three cells in a row with numbers. A cell is a supercell when its number is greater than each immediate neighbour. She wants only the middle cell to be a supercell.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: The filling 9, 4, 2 works, because only the left cell is a supercell.
options.B: The filling 4, 9, 2 works, because only the middle cell is greater than each immediate neighbour.
options.C: Any filling where 9 appears is enough, because 9 is the largest number she wrote.
options.D: The filling 2, 4, 9 works, because only the right cell is a supercell.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri looks at a number line from 3000 to 4000. The interval is divided into five equal parts with marks at equal spacing.

What number does the first mark after 3000 show?

options.A: 3001, treating each mark as one unit.
options.B: 3500, splitting the interval into two equal halves only.
options.D: 4000, jumping straight to the right endpoint.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Asha asks how many 1-digit counting numbers there are.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: There is 1 such number, because a 1-digit number is itself called a digit.
options.B: There are 10 such numbers, counting 0 through 9 without the chapter start at 1.
options.C: There are 9 such numbers: 1 through 9 each have digit length 1.
options.D: The same count also settles how many 2-digit numbers there are, with no further check.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yamini wants a 3-digit number whose digits add to 9.

Which number has digit sum 9?

options.A: 900, reading only the leading digit 9 as the digit sum.
options.B: 123, because 123 looks like the smallest neat 3-digit print.
options.D: 306, because 306 is greater than all its neighbouring cells in a grid.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qadir lists every whole number from $10$ to $19$. He wants the number of times the digit $1$ is written in that list.

Which count is correct?

options.A: Count $10$, $11$, $12$, $13$, $14$, $15$, $16$, $17$, $18$, and $19$ as ten hits, treating each number that contains a $1$ as a single hit.
options.B: Say that writing the digit $1$ is what creates the list from $10$ to $19$.
options.C: Count every written $1$: one in $10$, two in $11$, and one each in $12$ through $19$, for $11$ written ones.
options.D: Use the same $11$ also as the count of how many times $1$ appears from $1$ to $100$, with no further check.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Omkar wants a $3$-digit palindrome using digits from $1$ to $9$ only.

Which number is a $3$-digit palindrome?

options.A: $123$, claiming it is a palindrome even though the hundreds digit $1$ and the units digit $3$ differ.
options.B: Say that digits are what the palindrome label produces, so any $3$-digit number he likes counts.
options.C: $454$, because it reads the same forwards and backwards (hundreds digit equals units digit).
options.D: Treat $45$ as a $3$-digit palindrome by the same rule.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Indira starts with the $2$-digit number $23$. She reverses the digits and adds, then repeats reverse-and-add until she should stop.

Which claim applies the process correctly?

options.A: Form $23 + 32 = 55$, notice $55$ reads the same both ways, and keep reverse-and-adding anyway.
options.B: Say that reaching a palindrome is what creates the starting number $23$.
options.C: Form $23 + 32 = 55$; $55$ is a palindrome, so stop at $55$.
options.D: Repeat the chapter word palindrome alone, without reverse-and-adding $23$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri builds a $5$-digit palindrome. Its ten-thousands digit is $6$ and its hundreds digit is $2$. The thousands digit is half the ten-thousands digit.

Which number is it?

options.A: Call the answer the "thousands digit" label, without building the full palindrome.
options.B: Say the thousands digit is what produces the ten-thousands digit, reversing the given half-relation.
options.C: $63236$, because ten-thousands $=$ units $= 6$, thousands $=$ tens $= 3$ (half of $6$), and hundreds $= 2$.
options.D: Report $2$ alone, because that digit is printed as the hundreds clue.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Asha starts Kaprekar's $4$-digit routine with $6174$ (not all digits equal). She forms the largest and smallest arrangements of its digits and subtracts.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Form $7641 - 1467 = 6174$, then keep rearranging and subtracting as if the constant had not been reached.
options.B: Say that reaching $6174$ is what creates the digit arrangements of the starting number.
options.C: Form $7641 - 1467 = 6174$; the result is again $6174$, so the routine has reached Kaprekar's constant.
options.D: Repeat only the chapter word constant, without forming largest and smallest arrangements from the digits of $6174$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yamini searches a list of 12-hour clock times for a digit pattern: the four digits read the same forward and backward (a palindrome), and the time must be valid.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Accept $15$:$51$ as a palindrome time even though $15$ is not a valid hour on a 12-hour clock.
options.B: Say that calling a time a palindrome is what creates the written digits $1$, $2$, $2$, $1$, instead of reading those digits in order.
options.C: Keep $12$:$21$ — the digits $1,2,2,1$ read the same both ways, and $12$:$21$ is a valid 12-hour clock time.
options.D: Also require every calendar date in the same list to be a perfect square, beyond testing digit patterns in the clock times.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Uma wants to answer this question: which fruit do the students in Class 6A like most for the mid-day snack?

Which plan correctly sets up the inquiry?

options.A: Treat the words Class 6A as the answer, and collect no fruit choices.
options.B: Collect fresh fruit choices from some students, without naming Class 6A.
options.C: Collect fresh fruit choices from the students in Class 6A.
options.D: First choose a fruit Uma likes, then say that Class 6A likes that fruit.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sahil records favourite fruits from his row: mango, apple, mango, banana, apple, mango.

How should he find which fruit is most common?

options.A: Assign each answer to one fruit category and count the frequency in each category.
options.B: Leave the answers in the order he heard them and treat that list as the finished result.
options.C: Square the number of answers and report that square as the frequency of mango.
options.D: Multiply each fruit name by how often it appears to get a total amount, skipping the frequency table.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nalini has a frequency table that shows how many students chose each game for the sports day. She now wants to pair each student with the game that student chose.

What does she need?

options.A: The frequency table alone, because the table is already the list of individual student choices.
options.B: Only the frequency table, even though she must match each student to one game.
options.C: The individual records, because the frequency table keeps category totals but not which student chose which game.
options.D: A decorated chart title, because neat artwork is what makes the pairing possible.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The figure shows Komal's pictograph of books borrowed on three days. The key says each circle stands for 10 books.

How many more books were borrowed on Wednesday than on Tuesday?

options.A: 20 books, because Wednesday has 2 more circles than Tuesday and each circle is 10 books.
options.B: 2 books, equal to the difference in the number of circles.
options.C: 50 books, equal to Wednesday's total alone.
options.D: 5/3 books, from dividing Wednesday's circle count by Tuesday's.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ekta is drawing a pictograph of books read by four friends: $4$, $6$, $8$, and $10$. She wants fewer symbols on the page, but every count must still be shown exactly with whole symbols.

Which key should she choose?

options.A: Write the data values $4$, $6$, $8$, and $10$ as the pictograph key itself.
options.B: First invent a key, and say that key is what creates the four book counts.
options.C: Let each book symbol stand for $2$ books, because then $4$, $6$, $8$, and $10$ need $2$, $3$, $4$, and $5$ whole symbols.
options.D: Replace the pictograph with a frequency table alone, and treat that table as the finished pictograph key.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
The figure shows Chitra's bar graph of games played on three days. The vertical scale uses equal intervals.

Which day has the greatest number of games?

options.A: Monday, reading bar width instead of bar height on the numerical scale.
options.B: Tuesday, because its bar is tallest on the equal-interval scale.
options.C: Wednesday, comparing bars as if the vertical scale need not use equal intervals.
options.D: Monday, because that bar is shaded darker and decoration settles the value.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Uma records club players as Cricket $8$, Kho-kho $6$, and Football $4$. The figure shows the bar graph she wants to match that table.

Which plan constructs a valid bar graph from such category-value data?

options.A: Call the vertical axis the whole bar graph, without placing the three game categories or their bars.
options.B: Draw bars for Cricket, Kho-kho, and Football with unequal widths, skipping the equal-width rule.
options.C: Put the game categories on one axis, choose one uniform number scale on the other, and draw equal-width bars whose heights match $8$, $6$, and $4$ on that scale.
options.D: Pick the largest printed number $8$ from the table and treat that single number as the finished bar graph.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sahil's frequency table for coins collected shows outcomes $1$, $2$, and $5$ rupees with frequencies $4$, $3$, and $2$.

How should he find the total amount?

options.A: Add only the frequencies $4+3+2=9$, and report $9$ as the total amount in rupees.
options.B: Multiply and add $1\times 4+2\times 3+5\times 2$ even when the row labels are colour names instead of rupee amounts.
options.C: Compute $1\times 4+2\times 3+5\times 2=4+6+10=20$ rupees.
options.D: Say that the total amount is what creates the frequency of each outcome.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nalini measures the heights of three plants as $12$ cm, $18$ cm, and $9$ cm. The figure shows a display she is planning.

Which claim about orientation fits the kind of measurement?

options.A: Call the finished picture a vertical column label only, without matching display direction to how heights are compared.
options.B: Say that choosing upward columns is what creates the three plant heights $12$, $18$, and $9$ cm.
options.C: Use upward columns so taller plants read as taller bars, matching how height is naturally compared.
options.D: Pick the largest printed number $18$ alone and treat that single number as the finished display.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Komal sees a poster: School A has $20$ students drawn as a huge icon, and School B has $40$ students drawn as an icon only a little larger than A's, not about twice as tall.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Trust the poster because it looks appealing, skipping that icon sizes must match the counts.
options.B: Say that visual appeal is what creates the true counts $20$ and $40$.
options.C: Do not trust it as accurate: the icon sizes do not preserve the $20:40$ relationship.
options.D: Reject the poster only because it uses colour decoration that does not change how the data read.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Jatin needs a number that is a multiple of both 4 and 6.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: 8 is such a number, because 8 is a multiple of 4.
options.B: 2 is such a number, because 2 divides both 4 and 6.
options.C: 12 is such a number, because 12 is a multiple of 4 and of 6.
options.D: Any multiple of 4 alone is enough, even if it is not a multiple of 6.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Walia lists multiples of 4 as 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, ... and multiples of 6 as 6, 12, 18, 24, ...

What is the smallest common multiple of 4 and 6?
author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Bharat places a treasure on the number 24 on a number strip. He may jump by a fixed whole-number size from 0 and wants every jump to land exactly on 24.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: The answer is 24, because that is the treasure number itself.
options.B: Jump size 5 works, because repeated jumps of 5 stay on whole numbers.
options.C: Jump sizes 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 24 all land exactly on 24.
options.D: Jump size 24 is forced, because 24 is the largest printed mark on the strip.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Padma has two treasure numbers, $12$ and $18$. She may use only one jump size, repeated, and that jump size must land exactly on both treasures.

Which list gives every successful jump size?

options.A: $1$, $2$, $3$, $6$, $9$ — including $9$, which reaches $18$ only.
options.B: The common multiples of $12$ and $18$, because reaching both is what produces the factor list.
options.D: $4$ and $9$, each of which hits only one of the two treasures.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Jatin lists the factors of three whole numbers: $1$ has only $\{1\}$; $7$ has $\{1,7\}$; $12$ has $\{1,2,3,4,6,12\}$.

How should he classify $1$, $7$, and $12$?

options.A: Call $1$ a composite number, using the label composite instead of reading its factor count.
options.B: Say the prime/composite labels are what produce the factor lists, instead of reading the lists to decide the labels.
options.C: $1$ is neither (one factor); $7$ is prime (exactly two factors); $12$ is composite (more than two factors).
options.D: Treat the question as a jump-size treasure hunt on a number line, and classify from landing spots instead of factor counts.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri runs the Sieve of Eratosthenes on the whole numbers from $1$ to $20$.

Which statement is correct when the sieve is finished?

options.A: Call every uncrossed number the sieve method itself, without separating primes from composites.
options.B: Say the final circled primes are what produce the earlier crossing out of multiples.
options.C: $1$ is crossed out; each next uncrossed number is circled as prime and its later multiples are crossed out; circled numbers are primes and other crossed-out numbers are composites.
options.D: Find common factors of pairs such as $12$ and $18$, and treat that factor check as the sieve.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Walia checks whether $8$ and $9$ are co-prime by looking at their common factors.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call them a safe pair as a name only, without checking common factors of $8$ and $9$.
options.B: Say the co-prime decision is what creates the absence of a common factor greater than $1$, instead of checking factors first.
options.C: They are co-prime, because their only common factor is $1$.
options.D: Decide from the final digit alone, as in a divisibility-by-$2$ or $5$ check, without listing common factors of $8$ and $9$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Bharat ties thread on a circular board with $12$ pegs, stepping a fixed gap of $5$ pegs each time. He asks whether the thread will eventually reach every peg.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Answer "thread-gap", naming that phrase instead of checking whether $12$ and $5$ share a common factor.
options.B: Say that reaching every peg is what creates the co-primality of $12$ and $5$, instead of using co-primality to predict the reach.
options.C: Yes: $12$ and $5$ are co-prime, so stepping by $5$ visits every peg before repeating.
options.D: Treat the question as a treasure-pair hunt that only asks whether two numbers are co-prime, without linking that fact to the cyclic peg walk.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Padma writes $56=14\times 4$ and $63=21\times 3$. She asks whether that single pair of factorisations proves $56$ and $63$ have no common factor greater than $1$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Conclude they are co-prime from those two products alone, without checking whether another common factor was missed.
options.B: Say that calling them co-prime is what creates the incomplete factor listing, instead of testing all possible common factors.
options.C: No: one chosen factorisation of each number can miss a common factor; the search must account for every possible common factor.
options.D: Require a full prime-factorisation write-up of every integer as the only allowed method for this decision.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ekta writes $60 = 6 \times 10$ and wants the prime factorisation of $60$ by breaking composite factors until only primes remain.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Call the finished answer "prime factor" only, without writing the full product of primes for $60$.
options.B: Say that writing $2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 5$ is what creates the breaking of $6$ and $10$, instead of breaking those composites first.
options.C: Replace $6$ by $2 \times 3$ and $10$ by $2 \times 5$, so $60 = 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 5$ with only primes left.
options.D: Fill a different prime product-grid puzzle for every row and column, and treat that puzzle as this factor-breaking of $60$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Chitra writes $60 = 2\times 2\times 3\times 5$ and also $60 = 2^{2}\times 3\times 5$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the answer order of factors, without deciding whether the two prime factorisations are the same.
options.B: Say that having the same product $60$ is what creates the matching primes with the same repetitions.
options.C: $2\times 2\times 3\times 5$ and $2^{2}\times 3\times 5$ are the same prime factorisation; order and grouping do not change it.
options.D: Decide they differ only because one printed form uses an exponent and the other writes two $2$s.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Mona's rectangular garden is 8 m long and 5 m wide. She wants the distance around the garden once, along the boundary.

What is that distance?
author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Farhan's rectangular playground has perimeter 30 m. One side is 9 m long.

What is the length of the adjacent side?

options.C: 6 m

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Wasim's triangular flower bed has side lengths 5 m, 7 m, and 9 m.

What is its perimeter?

options.A: 7 m, taking the middle side length as the perimeter.
options.B: Each side equals 21 m, because the perimeter produces each side.
options.C: 21 m, by adding the three side lengths.
options.D: 3 m, because a triangle is named by having three sides.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nitin's square courtyard has each side $6$ m long.

Which calculation gives its perimeter?

options.A: Call the shape an equilateral triangle, and use $3 \times 6$.
options.B: Use $4 \times 6$ even if two sides were a different length.
options.C: $4 \times 6 = 24$ m, because all four sides are equal.
options.D: $6$ m, taking the printed side length on the plan as the perimeter.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Farhan runs on a rectangular track whose perimeter is $400$ m. He runs $950$ m from a start mark.

Which claim about full rounds and leftover distance is correct?

options.A: Call "one round" the leftover distance, without using the perimeter.
options.B: Convert using $400$ m even if the actual track perimeter were a different length.
options.C: Full rounds $= 2$ and leftover $= 150$ m along the track, because $950 = 2 \times 400 + 150$.
options.D: Report $950$ alone, because that numeral is printed largest.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Soham traces a path on square-grid paper. One segment runs $3$ straight grid units along the lines; the next segment cuts diagonally across one square.

Which claim about the path length is correct?

options.A: Call the answer grid path only, without separating straight and diagonal lengths.
options.B: Count the diagonal cut as $1$ grid unit, the same as a straight side, with no separate estimate.
options.C: Measure the straight parts in grid units and treat the diagonal as longer than one straight grid unit, then add the lengths.
options.D: Say that calling the diagonal longer is what creates the grid path itself.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ekta has two $3$ cm by $2$ cm rectangles. She joins them along a shared $2$ cm edge and asks how the perimeter changes.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the answer "joined arrangement" only, without measuring the new outside boundary.
options.B: Add the two separate perimeters in full, counting the touching $2$ cm edges as if they were still outside.
options.C: After the join, the touching $2$ cm edges are inside, so the new perimeter is $16$ cm (a $6$ cm by $2$ cm rectangle), not $20$ cm.
options.D: Say that the new $16$ cm perimeter is what creates the joining along the $2$ cm edge, instead of joining first and then reading the outside boundary.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ritu shares the same chapati equally. She compares the unit fractions 1/6 and 1/8 from that whole.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: 1/8 is greater than 1/6 because 8 is greater than 6.
options.B: 1/6 is greater than 1/8 because fewer equal shares make each share larger.
options.C: 1/6 and 1/8 are equal because each numerator is 1.
options.D: 1/8 is greater because the denominator is the size of the share.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Mona and Nitin each start with the same whole chapati. Mona cuts hers into 4 equal pieces. Nitin cuts his into 4 pieces of different sizes. Each takes one piece and calls it one-fourth of the chapati.

Whose piece is a valid fractional unit of one-fourth?

options.A: Only Mona's piece, because the parts must be equal in size.
options.B: Both pieces, because each chapati was cut into 4 pieces.
options.C: Only Nitin's piece, because unequal shapes still make fourths.
options.D: Neither piece, because fourths must be triangles.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Javed places the fraction 3/4 on a number line marked from 0 to 1.

Which plan places 3/4 correctly?

options.A: Divide the interval from 0 to 1 into 4 equal lengths and count 3 of those lengths from 0.
options.B: Mark a point near 1 because the printed 4 looks large, without making equal lengths.
options.C: Place 3/4 by comparing only how large 3 looks next to 4 on the page.
options.D: The number-line placement rule also requires changing 3/4 into another kind of number first.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Harish has the improper fraction 17/5 and wants it as a mixed number.

Which mixed number is correct?
author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Bharat has the fraction 2/3 of a chapati. He wants another fraction for the same quantity of that chapati.

Which plan gives an equivalent fraction?

options.A: Change only the numerator to 4 and keep the denominator 3.
options.B: Multiply numerator and denominator by the same nonzero number, for example write 4/6.
options.C: Write 4/6 even when the new pair is no longer about the same chapati.
options.D: First convert 2/3 into a decimal; equivalence requires that conversion.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Zaid reduces the fraction 18/24 to lowest terms.

Which result is correct?

options.A: 6, reporting the common factor as the answer.
options.B: 6/1, because lowest terms are said to produce the common factor.
options.C: 3/4, by dividing numerator and denominator by 6.
options.D: 18, by counting how many 1/24-units make up 18/24.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ritu must decide which is larger, $\dfrac{3}{4}$ or $\dfrac{5}{6}$.

Which plan compares them correctly?

options.A: Call the answer equivalent fractions, without comparing the two given fractions.
options.B: First invent which fraction is larger, and say that choice is what creates a common denominator.
options.C: Rewrite both with denominator $12$ as $\dfrac{9}{12}$ and $\dfrac{10}{12}$, then compare the numerators $9$ and $10$.
options.D: Convert each fraction to a percent first, and compare only after that conversion.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Parul adds $\frac{2}{7}$ and $\frac{3}{7}$.

How should she find the sum?

options.A: Call the shared denominator the sum, without adding the numerator counts.
options.B: Say that adding the fractions is what creates the common denominator after the fact.
options.C: Keep the denominator $7$ and add the numerators: $\frac{2}{7} + \frac{3}{7} = \frac{5}{7}$.
options.D: Report $3$ alone because that numeral is printed largest in the second fraction.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Javed must compute $\dfrac{5}{6} - \dfrac{1}{4}$.

Which plan subtracts the fractions correctly?

options.A: Call the answer same denominator, without finding the value of the difference.
options.B: Subtract as $\dfrac{5-1}{6-4} = \dfrac{4}{2}$, skipping common-denominator alignment.
options.C: Rewrite as $\dfrac{10}{12} - \dfrac{3}{12} = \dfrac{7}{12}$.
options.D: Say that the difference $\dfrac{7}{12}$ is what creates the common denominator $12$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Harish rewrites $\frac{2}{3}$ with denominator $12$ so he can add it to $\frac{5}{12}$.

Why must the numerator change along with the denominator?

options.A: Call the result an "equivalent fraction" label while keeping numerator $2$ and only writing denominator $12$.
options.B: Change the denominator to $12$ without multiplying the numerator by the same factor.
options.C: Multiply numerator and denominator by the same factor $4$: $\frac{2}{3} = \frac{8}{12}$, so the value is unchanged for the common-denominator sum.
options.D: Say the equivalent fraction is what produces the common denominator after the fact.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Wasim chooses the unit $\dfrac{1}{5}$ metre and finds that a ribbon is covered by exactly $7$ such units.

Which claim measures the ribbon correctly?

options.A: Report the length as $\dfrac{7}{5}$ metre even if the unit length changes mid-count, without keeping one fixed metre as the whole.
options.B: Say that writing $\dfrac{7}{5}$ metre is what creates the seven copies of $\dfrac{1}{5}$ metre.
options.C: Count $7$ copies of the unit $\dfrac{1}{5}$ metre, so the ribbon length is $\dfrac{7}{5}$ metre.
options.D: Also treat the same $7$ copies as settling the ribbon's area in square metres, beyond this length count.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Vivek opens a compass to a fixed length, keeps the metal point fixed at P, and moves only the pencil.

What path does the pencil draw?

options.A: A circle whose radius is the point P.
options.B: A circle with centre at the moving pencil tip, and with P on the rim.
options.C: A circle with centre P, and with every pencil point at the same fixed distance from P.
options.D: A square that has one corner fixed at P.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tanya wants a circular hole of radius 2 cm at the centre of a square card of side 10 cm. She will use a compass.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Place the compass tip at a corner of the square and set the radius to 2 cm.
options.B: Place the tip anywhere on the card; only setting the radius to 2 cm matters.
options.C: Place the tip at the centre of the square and set the radius to 2 cm.
options.D: Draw the curve freehand without a fixed centre, because neat artwork is enough.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Omkar studies the four-sided figure drawn below. It is tilted on the page. Every side is $3$ cm, and every corner is $90^\circ$.

What is the figure?

options.A: A rectangle only, because any four-sided shape with right angles is called a rectangle and not a square.
options.B: A square, from the equal sides alone, without using the right-angle marks.
options.C: A square, because all sides are equal and all angles are $90^\circ$, even though it is rotated.
options.D: Not a square, because rotating the shape is what changes its side lengths and angles.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit labels the corners of a rectangle A, B, C, D in order going around the boundary. A valid name may start at any corner and then follow that travel order.

Which name is valid for that rectangle?

options.A: Rectangle ACDB, listing corners by jumping across instead of travelling the boundary.
options.B: Only rectangle ABCD is allowed; starting at any other corner makes the name invalid.
options.C: Rectangle ABCD is valid only after renaming the corners in alphabetical order first.
options.D: Rectangle BCDA is valid: it lists corners in boundary travel order, starting at B.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Farid must construct a square of side $5$ cm with ruler and compass.

Which plan forces the square?

options.A: Draw a base of $5$ cm and raise perpendiculars at both ends, but mark any new lengths on those perpendiculars.
options.B: First draw the upright sides, and say those upright sides are what create the $5$ cm base.
options.C: Draw base AB of $5$ cm, construct a perpendicular at A and at B, mark $5$ cm on each perpendicular to get D and C, then join DC.
options.D: Find the area $25$ cm$^{2}$ first, and treat that area calculation as the construction of the square.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Deepak draws rectangle ABCD. Point X moves on side AD and point Y moves on side BC. He wants to track how near or far X and Y are.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Track only the position of Y; the position of X is not needed.
options.B: Nearness can be decided without placing X on AD and Y on BC.
options.C: Measure the length of segment XY; that length changes as X and Y move.
options.D: X and Y are near when the printed letters look close on the page.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Vivek must divide a $6$ cm by $4$ cm rectangle into identical squares that fill the rectangle with no gaps.

Which claim correctly plans the equal segments?

options.A: Mark any set of cuts across the $6$ cm side alone, and skip making every square side equal.
options.B: First draw the finished identical squares, and say those squares are what create the $6$ cm and $4$ cm sides.
options.C: Choose a common side length that divides both $6$ cm and $4$ cm, then cut so every square has all four sides equal to that length.
options.D: First find the rectangle's area $24$ cm$^{2}$, and treat that area formula as the tiling into identical squares.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tanya draws rectangle PQRS. She wants to explore its diagonals by length and by the angles they make.

Which plan starts the comparison correctly?

options.A: Compare side PQ with side QR only, without joining any opposite corners.
options.B: Say that drawing the diagonals is what creates rectangle PQRS.
options.C: Join opposite corners to form diagonals PR and QS, then compare those lengths and the angles they form.
options.D: Also prove the general diagonal laws for every parallelogram, as if that proof were required for this exploration.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Omkar must construct rectangle $ABCD$ so that diagonal $AC$ divides $\angle DAB$ into $60^\circ$ and $30^\circ$.

Which plan locates the next sides and vertex $D$ correctly?

options.A: Call the finished figure diagonal $AC$ only, without using the right angle at $A$ or the $60^\circ$ and $30^\circ$ parts.
options.B: Say that drawing diagonal $AC$ is what creates rectangle $ABCD$, instead of building the rectangle from right angles and equal opposite sides.
options.C: Use $\angle DAB=90^\circ$, so the $60^\circ$ part leaves $30^\circ$; then place $D$ with right angles (or equal opposite sides) from the known sides.
options.D: Choose the plan only because $60$ is the largest printed angle number among $60$ and $30$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit must construct rectangle $ABCD$ given side $DC = 5$ cm and diagonal $DB = 7$ cm.

Which plan locates vertex $B$ correctly?

options.A: Erect a perpendicular at $C$ without first drawing side $DC$ at its given length $5$ cm.
options.B: Locate $B$ by trial-and-error with a ruler only, without using a perpendicular and an arc.
options.C: Draw $DC$; erect a perpendicular to $DC$ at $C$; from $D$ draw an arc of radius $7$ cm; $B$ is their intersection.
options.D: Place $B$ using only the printed length $5$ cm, ignoring the diagonal length $7$ cm.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Bharat must locate a point that is $5$ cm from point $B$ and $5$ cm from point $C$.

Which plan finds that point correctly?

options.A: Call the answer point $B$, without locating an intersection of equal-radius arcs.
options.B: Say that the intersection point is what creates the given points $B$ and $C$.
options.C: Draw an arc of radius $5$ cm centred at $B$ and an arc of radius $5$ cm centred at $C$; a required point is their intersection.
options.D: Choose a point only because the printed length $5$ cm stands out, without drawing the equal-radius arcs.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Kavya has a paper square with a design on it. She wants to know whether the design has mathematical symmetry.

Which check decides that?

options.A: The design looks attractive, so it is symmetric.
options.B: The design has matching colours, so it is symmetric.
options.C: A fold or a turn maps the design onto itself.
options.D: A definite pattern of matching parts is what creates symmetry by itself.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Xavier has a paper heart and a possible vertical mid-line drawn on it.

When is that mid-line a line of symmetry?

options.A: Whenever the heart looks roughly balanced, even if it is never folded.
options.B: When folding along the mid-line is treated as a result produced by an already known line of symmetry.
options.C: Only when folding along that mid-line makes the two parts overlap exactly point for point.
options.D: Only when a group-theory symmetry order of 2 is named for the heart.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Chitra draws the square shown in the figure. She wants to count its lines of symmetry by testing folds.

How many lines of symmetry does the square have?

options.A: Infinitely many, because any line through the centre looks balanced at a glance.
options.B: Four folds are what create the square in the first place.
options.C: Four: two through midpoints of opposite sides and two through opposite corners, each passing the fold test.
options.D: The count needs group-theory language before any fold can be checked.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qasim is completing a mirror image across a fixed vertical symmetry line. Point A is $2$ cm to the left of the line, at a marked height.

Where does the reflected point A' belong?

options.A: A' is the name mirror image for the symmetry line itself.
options.B: A' may sit anywhere on the right of the line, at any distance.
options.C: A' is $2$ cm to the right of the line, at the same height as A.
options.D: First place A', and that placement is what creates the symmetry line.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Soham folds the square sheet in the figure once down the middle, punches one hole through both layers, then unfolds the sheet.

Which claim correctly predicts the unfolded design?

options.A: The fold line itself is the punched design.
options.B: One hole appears anywhere on the paper, even where the layers did not meet.
options.C: Two holes appear as mirror images across the fold line, because the fold forced matching positions to coincide.
options.D: The punched holes are what create the fold line.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Hassan studies the equilateral triangle in the figure below, with centre O marked.

Does the triangle have rotational symmetry?

options.A: Call O the name rotational symmetry, without testing any turn of the triangle.
options.B: Say the centre O is what the matching turn creates, instead of using O to test a turn.
options.C: Yes, because a turn of $120^\circ$ about O makes the triangle coincide with itself, and $120^\circ$ is less than a full turn.
options.D: Count three equal sides and report the order of rotational symmetry from that count alone, without naming a turn angle less than $360^\circ$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Komal studies the regular hexagon in the figure. It is divided into $6$ equal triangular parts meeting at the centre O.

What is the smallest angle of rotational symmetry, and what is the order?

options.A: Any turn about O works, even if the six parts are not equal or equally spaced.
options.B: She must use group-theory language about rotation groups before naming an angle or order.
options.C: The smallest angle is $360^\circ/6 = 60^\circ$, and the order is $6$.
options.D: She should test only for a mirror line through O, and treat that line test as the rotational order.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Xavier asks why a circle is a special limiting case for line symmetry and rotational symmetry.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Say the circle matches itself after some turn, but skip that the turn is about the centre and that every diameter is a symmetry line.
options.B: Say the centre is what the circle creates, instead of using the centre to test turns and diameters.
options.C: A circle matches itself after a turn by any angle about its centre, and every diameter is a line of symmetry, so it has infinitely many rotational symmetries and infinitely many symmetry lines.
options.D: Require group-theory language about symmetry groups, beyond line and turn matching for the circle.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Chitra has a paper cut-out of a capital letter S. She wants to decide whether it has line symmetry and whether it has rotational symmetry.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Answer "rotational symmetry" alone, naming that label instead of running both tests.
options.B: Decide from a single glance that whatever is true of one kind of symmetry is automatically true of the other.
options.C: Apply the fold test for line symmetry and the turn test for rotational symmetry separately; the letter may have one, both, or neither.
options.D: Pick the answer from the printed word "letter" in the stem, without folding or turning the cut-out.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Nitin marks three temperatures on a number line with 0 as the reference: −3 °C, 0 °C, and 4 °C.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: −3 °C is below zero, 4 °C is above zero, and 0 °C is neither positive nor negative.
options.B: 0 °C is a positive temperature because it is written without a minus sign.
options.C: −3 °C is above zero, and 4 °C is below zero.
options.D: −3 °C and 4 °C are the same kind of signed value because both sit away from zero.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri places −7, −2, and 3 on a number line with 0 marked.

Which statement about their order is correct?

options.A: −7 is greater than −2 because 7 is greater than 2.
options.B: −2 is farther left than −7, so −2 is smaller.
options.C: −7 is farther left than −2, so −7 is smaller than −2, and both are smaller than 3.
options.D: 3 is smaller than −7 because it is written with fewer digits.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yamini stands at +3 on a number line and then moves −5.

Where does she finish?

options.A: −5, reporting only the movement.
options.B: +8, by adding 3 and 5 as same-direction jumps on a sparse unmarked line.
options.C: −2, because start + movement = 3 + (−5).
options.D: 28, by computing 3 + 5².

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Omkar stands at $+2$ on a number line. He wants to reach $-4$.

What signed movement does he need?

options.A: Call $-4$ the needed movement, without using the start.
options.B: Say the needed movement is what produces the start $+2$ after he arrives.
options.C: $-6$, because target $-$ start $= -4 - (+2)$.
options.D: Treat the jump as a place-value regrouping of $2$ and $4$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri needs the additive inverse of $-7$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call "opposite integer" the finished answer, without naming the number that cancels $-7$.
options.B: Say $+7$ even if the two numbers did not have equal distance from zero.
options.C: $+7$, because $(-7)+(+7)=0$ (same distance from zero, opposite sign).
options.D: Report $7$ alone, because that digit is printed in $-7$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qasim must rewrite $6-(-2)$ as addition of an inverse.

Which rewrite is correct?

options.A: Call the answer additive inverse only, without rewriting the subtraction as an addition.
options.B: Say that writing $6+(+2)$ is what creates the expression $6-(-2)$, instead of starting from the subtraction.
options.C: Write $6-(-2)=6+(+2)$, because subtracting $-2$ is adding the additive inverse of $-2$.
options.D: Find the signed move from $6$ to $-2$ on a number line, and treat that target-minus-start rule as this rewrite.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Farid must compute $248 + 175$ on a sparse number line that shows only $0$, $248$, and a few jump marks — not every integer.

Which plan fits that line?

options.A: Call the method "large integers" only, without using jumps from $248$ on the sparse marks.
options.B: Say that the finished sum $423$ is what creates the sparse jump marks, instead of using those marks to find the sum.
options.C: From $248$, jump $+100$, then $+70$, then $+5$ (or other jumps that total $+175$) using only the needed marks, landing on $423$.
options.D: Choose $248$ as the sum only because $248$ is the largest printed mark among $0$, $248$, and the jump labels.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Farid has $5$ positive tokens and $3$ negative tokens. He adds them by cancelling zero pairs.

What sum should he report?

options.A: Call the answer "negative token" only, without cancelling zero pairs among the $5$ positive and $3$ negative tokens.
options.B: Add $5+3=8$ and report $8$, skipping that each positive-negative pair cancels to zero.
options.C: Cancel $3$ zero pairs; $2$ positive tokens remain, so the sum is $+2$.
options.D: Report $5$ alone, because $5$ is the larger printed token count among $5$ and $3$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sahil writes the successor of 99,999 and names the place-value unit.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: The successor is 99,998.
options.B: The successor is 1,00,000, which is one crore.
options.C: The successor is 1,00,000, which is one lakh (1 followed by 5 zeroes).
options.D: 99,999 already counts as one lakh because it looks nearly as large.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Komal hears the number one lakh and asks whether that number is big or small. She can compare with familiar sizes such as people in a stadium or days in a lifetime.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: One lakh is always big, because the words "one lakh" sound large by themselves.
options.B: The familiar comparison is produced by one lakh first, so the number chooses the setting.
options.C: Decide only after naming what is counted and comparing with a familiar size.
options.D: One lakh is always small, because the same digits can be rearranged to look shorter.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Chitra's school building is 20 m tall. A classroom door in the same building is about 2 m tall. She wants to make sense of the 20 m height.

Which comparison is appropriate?

options.A: Read only the printed 20 and skip naming any familiar object for comparison.
options.B: Decide from place-value naming of the digits in 20 alone, without a familiar height.
options.C: Compare with the door: the building is about 10 door-heights, or 18 m taller than the door.
options.D: Choose 20 because it is the largest printed number in the stem.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Sahil must write $50821693$ with commas in the Indian system and then read it.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Place commas in threes as $50,821,693$ and read it with million and billion as the Indian reading.
options.B: Write $5,08,21,693$ with no reading in words, and treat the commas alone as finishing the task.
options.C: Write $5,08,21,693$ and read five crore eight lakh twenty-one thousand six hundred ninety-three.
options.D: Say that placing Indian commas is what creates the digit string $50821693$ itself.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Komal's calculator starts at $0$ and has only a $+100$ button. She wants the display to show exactly $700$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the answer presses, without finding how many $+100$ taps make $700$.
options.B: Mix $+10$ and $+100$ taps, even though only the $+100$ button is available.
options.C: Press $+100$ seven times, because $700 \div 100 = 7$.
options.D: Invent a multi-button breakdown such as five $+100$ taps and twenty $+10$ taps.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tara's calculator starts at $0$ and has buttons $+1$, $+10$, $+100$, and $+1000$. She wants the display to show exactly $240$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the answer place-value buttons only, without saying which presses make $240$.
options.B: Say that reaching $240$ is what creates the $+10$ and $+100$ buttons.
options.C: Press $+100$ twice and $+10$ four times (or any regrouping that totals $240$), because many click mixes of powers of ten can make the same number.
options.D: Treat each button as multiplying the display by $10$, as if that were the same as adding powers of ten.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri's calculator starts at $0$ and has only $+1$, $+10$, $+100$, and $+1000$ buttons. She wants the display to show exactly $304$ with the fewest clicks.

Which plan is correct?

options.A: Press $+100$ three times and stop, skipping the ones-place clicks still needed for $304$.
options.B: Also allow a multiply button or other operations, beyond using only the powers-of-ten buttons from $0$.
options.C: Use place value: three $+100$ clicks and four $+1$ clicks, so $3+4=7$ clicks total (the digit sum).
options.D: Press $+1$ exactly $304$ times only because $304$ is the printed target on the display.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Walia buys 3 notebooks at Rs 20 each and pays with a Rs 100 note. She writes $100 - 3 \times 20$ for the change she should receive.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: 40 is the expression; $100 - 3 \times 20$ is only a name for that value.
options.B: $100 - 3 \times 20$ is an expression, but it has no value until an equals sign is written beside it.
options.C: $100 - 3 \times 20$ is an arithmetic expression for the change, and its value is 40.
options.D: The expression must be the printed 100 alone, because 100 is the largest number she sees.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Padma writes the two expressions $7 + 5$ and $3 \times 4$.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: 12 is the comparison sign between the two expressions.
options.B: The expressions can be ordered without finding either value.
options.C: $7 + 5 = 3 \times 4$, because both expressions have value 12.
options.D: She should also compare the separate decimals $7.0$ and $5.0$ before deciding.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri must evaluate $3 \times (8 - 5) + 2$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the word grouping the answer, without evaluating any part of the expression.
options.B: Ignore the brackets and evaluate as if the expression were unbracketed term by term from left to right only.
options.C: First evaluate $8 - 5$ inside the brackets to get $3$, then compute $3 \times 3 + 2 = 11$.
options.D: Multiply $3 \times 8$ first, then subtract $5$, giving $19$ after adding $2$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Walia studies the expression $83 - 14$.

What are its terms?

options.A: Call the plus-sign idea the terms, without naming the parts of $83 - 14$.
options.B: Say the listed terms are what create the expression $83 - 14$, instead of reading terms from the written expression.
options.C: Rewrite as $83 + (-14)$; the terms are $83$ and $-14$.
options.D: Report only the printed digits $8$, $3$, $1$, and $4$ as the terms, ignoring how $83 - 14$ is grouped.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Padma must evaluate the unbracketed expression $7 + 3 \times 4 - 2$.

Which order is correct?

options.A: Call the answer multiplication only, without evaluating each term and then combining the terms.
options.B: Work strictly left to right as $((7+3)\times 4)-2$, as if brackets already fixed that order.
options.C: First form the terms: compute $3\times 4=12$, then evaluate $7+12-2=17$.
options.D: Also treat an exponent such as $2^{3}$ under the same left-to-right walk, as if this hinge settled powers.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Yamini has rewritten an expression as the sum of terms $5 + (-3) + 8$.

Which claim about rearranging is correct?

options.A: Swap and group the terms freely even while a subtraction sign still sits between unsigned parts, without first writing signed terms.
options.B: Also claim that regrouping $(5+(-3))+8$ changes products such as $5\times(-3)\times 8$ the same way, as if products followed this sum rule.
options.C: Once the expression is a sum of terms, any order or grouping of $5$, $-3$, and $8$ keeps the same value, such as $5+8+(-3)$ or $(5+8)+(-3)$.
options.D: Decide only because $8$ is the largest printed number among $5$, $-3$, and $8$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Uday must remove the brackets in $8-(3-5)$.

Which rewrite is correct?

options.A: Call the step remove brackets only, without changing any signs inside.
options.B: Write $8-(3-5)=8-3-5$, keeping the inner signs as if no minus preceded the brackets.
options.C: Write $8-(3-5)=8-3+5$, because a minus before the brackets flips each inner sign.
options.D: Apply the same sign flip when removing brackets in $8+(3-5)$, where a plus precedes the brackets.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit measures a pencil on a ruler marked in centimetres. The tip ends between the 7 cm and 8 cm marks.

What should he do to report the length more accurately?

options.A: Report 7 cm, because the tip has not reached 8 cm.
options.B: Split the gap into unequal marks of any sizes he likes.
options.C: Split the 1 cm gap into equal smaller parts and count how many the tip passes.
options.D: Ignore the ruler marks and use only the printed number 7 on the pencil.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Dev has a length of 3 tenths of a metre on a measuring strip marked in tenths and hundredths.

Which statement describes the same length?

options.A: The length is 3 hundredths of a metre.
options.B: The length is 3 thousandths of a metre, ignoring regrouping by tens.
options.C: The length is 30 hundredths of a metre, because ten hundredths make one tenth.
options.D: The length is 3 metres, because the strip shows the digit 3 most clearly.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tara reads the length 3.142 m on a measuring strip marked with a decimal point.

Which statement correctly names the place of each digit?

options.A: The digit 3 is a tenth, because it sits next to the decimal point.
options.B: The length is 3142 m, because those digits are the largest printed string on the strip.
options.C: 3 is ones; 1 is tenths; 4 is hundredths; 2 is thousandths, with the decimal point separating whole-number places from fractional places.
options.D: Add the digits 3 + 1 + 4 + 2 by combining like place values to read the number.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit measures a ribbon as $45$ millimetres long. He needs the length in centimetres. There are $10$ millimetres in $1$ centimetre.

Which conversion is correct?

options.A: Report the answer as "centimetre", naming the unit instead of writing the decimal length.
options.B: Say that centimetres are what produce millimetres, so he must invent $45$ mm from a finished centimetre reading.
options.C: $45$ mm $= 4.5$ cm, because each millimetre is $0.1$ of a centimetre.
options.D: Write $45$ cm, copying the printed digits $45$ without shifting by the $10$-to-$1$ place relation.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Dev must mark $2.7$ on a number line that already shows the whole numbers $2$ and $3$.

How should he place $2.7$?

options.A: Answer "endpoint", naming that word instead of placing a mark between $2$ and $3$.
options.B: Say the finished mark is what creates the equal tenths between $2$ and $3$, instead of using those tenths to locate $2.7$.
options.C: Split the segment from $2$ to $3$ into $10$ equal tenths and count $7$ tenths from $2$ toward $3$.
options.D: Copy the printed digit $7$ and put the mark at $7$ on the number line, ignoring the interval from $2$ to $3$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Chitra compares the decimals $0.58$ and $0.6$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the answer first unequal digit, without deciding which decimal is larger.
options.B: Say $0.58 > 0.6$ because $0.58$ has more digits written after the decimal point.
options.C: Align place values as $0.58$ and $0.60$; in the tenths place $6 > 5$, so $0.6 > 0.58$.
options.D: Round both to the nearest whole number and compare those integers instead.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Zaid must choose which of $2.4$, $2.8$, and $3.1$ is closest to the target $2.75$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the answer distance only, without comparing each option to $2.75$.
options.B: Say that naming $2.8$ as closest is what creates the target $2.75$, instead of measuring distances from $2.75$.
options.D: Choose $3.1$ only because $3.1$ is the largest printed option among $2.4$, $2.8$, and $3.1$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Parul has m marbles. She buys 5 more and then gives 3 to a friend.

Which expression shows how many marbles she has now?

options.B: marbles + 5 − 3

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Harish evaluates the expression 3a + 2b when a = 4 and b = 5.

What value does he obtain?

options.A: 3 + 2, by dropping a and b.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Zaid meets the compact writings 5u and 10(y − 3) in his algebra notebook.

How should he read them before any calculation?

options.A: 5u names an 'omitted multiplication sign' rather than five times u.
options.B: 5u means 5 + u, because the multiplication idea can be dropped.
options.C: 5u means 5 × u, and 10(y − 3) means 10 times the whole of (y − 3).
options.D: The value is whichever numeral appears first in the writing.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Parul simplifies $3a + 5 + 2a - 1$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call 'like terms' the finished value, without combining anything.
options.B: Combine $3a + 5$ as like terms, dropping that only matching letter parts combine and that each sign stays with its term.
options.C: $3a$ and $2a$ are like terms, and $5$ and $-1$ are like terms, so the expression becomes $5a + 4$.
options.D: Combine using only the numeral $3$ printed first.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Harish simplifies $2(3x + 4) - (x - 5)$.

How should the brackets be removed before combining like terms?

options.A: Multiply $2$ only by the first term $3x$, skipping that every term inside the bracket is multiplied.
options.B: Use the same bracket rule to decide which chapter illustration to colour.
options.C: Distribute $2$ to every term inside, and change every term inside the subtracted bracket to its opposite: $6x + 8 - x + 5 = 5x + 13$.
options.D: Report $2$ alone, because that numeral is printed first.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Gauri compares the algebraic expressions $2(n+3)$ and $2n+6$.

When may she treat them as equal?

options.A: Call them "same value" as a label only, without checking values of $n$ or rewriting one expression into the other.
options.B: Treat them as equal after checking only $n=1$, skipping that equality must hold for every value of $n$ (or by a valid rewrite).
options.C: They are equal: distribute to get $2(n+3)=2n+6$, so both give the same value for every $n$.
options.D: Use the same equality test to decide whether two unrelated geometric figures are congruent.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Deepak's growing pattern has $3$ dots at Step $1$, and each next step adds $2$ dots.

Which claim gives a formula that works for any Step $y$?

options.A: Count $y$ increases of $2$ after Step $1$, instead of $y-1$ increases, when writing the formula.
options.B: Say that the general formula is what creates the observed step totals $3$, $5$, $7$, $\ldots$.
options.C: For Step $y$ there are $y-1$ increases of $2$ after Step $1$, so the total is $3+2(y-1)$.
options.D: Replace the growing-pattern formula with a cyclic remainder rule.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tanya draws two straight lines on her notebook page. The lines meet at exactly one point.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: The lines are intersecting, and their meeting point forms four angles.
options.B: Two straight lines can meet at two different points if she extends them far enough.
options.C: Meeting at one point means the lines are parallel.
options.D: Two straight lines that meet need not form any angles at the meeting point.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit draws two straight lines that meet at a point. One of the angles at the meeting point measures 70°. He needs the adjacent angle that sits on the same straight line with that 70° angle.

Which measure is correct?

options.A: 70°, because adjacent angles on that straight line must be equal.
options.D: 110°, because a linear pair on a straight line adds to 180°, so 180° − 70° = 110°.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Deepak draws two straight lines that cross at one point. One of the four angles at the crossing measures 65°.

What is the measure of the angle vertically opposite that 65° angle?

options.A: 65°, because vertically opposite angles at the same intersection are equal.
options.B: 115°, treating an adjacent angle on a straight line as if it were the vertically opposite angle.
options.C: 65°, because the angles may be called opposite angles that must sum to 180°.
options.D: 65°, only because 65 is already printed, without using the opposite-pair test.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Tanya draws two lines that meet at a point. All four angles at that meeting are equal.

What can she conclude?

options.A: Each angle is a right angle, and that label alone is the full conclusion.
options.B: The lines are perpendicular even when they stay apart and never meet.
options.C: The lines are perpendicular, because four equal angles at an intersection are each $90^\circ$.
options.D: The lines are perpendicular because the printed word equal is the standout word in the stem.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Lalit draws two straight lines on the same flat board. However far he extends them, they never meet, and the distance between them stays the same.

What can he conclude?

options.A: Call them same plane as the full answer, without deciding whether they are parallel.
options.B: Call them parallel even if they need not lie on the same plane.
options.C: The lines are parallel: they lie on the same plane and do not meet when extended.
options.D: Call them parallel only because the printed word distance stands out in the stem.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Uday studies the figure. Lines $p$ and $q$ each carry a single arrow mark. Lines $r$ and $s$ meet with a small square at the meeting point.

Which reading of the marks is correct?

options.A: Call the marks labels only, without saying what parallel or perpendicular relation they show.
options.B: Treat the small square as marking any acute angle, skipping that it marks a right angle.
options.C: The matching single arrow marks show $p \parallel q$, and the small square shows that $r$ is perpendicular to $s$.
options.D: Say that drawing the arrow marks is what creates lines $p$ and $q$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Hassan draws line $t$ that crosses lines $p$ and $q$ at two different points. He wants to identify the transversal and organise the angles formed.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the answer "two lines" only, without identifying $t$ as the transversal of $p$ and $q$.
options.B: Call $t$ a transversal even if it met only one of $p$ or $q$, skipping that a transversal must intersect two different lines.
options.C: $t$ is a transversal of $p$ and $q$; it forms eight angles, with vertically opposite equal pairs at each crossing.
options.D: Say that the eight angles are what create transversal $t$, instead of $t$ crossing $p$ and $q$ first.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Xavier lines up four children left to right with heights 140 cm, 150 cm, 145 cm, and 155 cm. Each child calls out how many taller children stand in front of that child.

Which height-code is correct?
author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qasim adds the scores $3$, $8$, $5$, $2$, and $7$ from five short games. He wants the parity of the total without adding all the values.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The answer is the word odd, because odd is the label that belongs on any parity question.
options.B: The total is even, because even scores appear in the list.
options.C: The total is odd, because there are three odd addends.
options.D: He should split the scores into short and long rhythms instead of counting odd addends.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Hassan has five odd-numbered cards. He wants to place all five cards so that their sum is exactly $30$.

What can he decide before trying any cases?

options.A: Call possible selection the answer, without using odd and even.
options.B: Treat the total $30$ as reachable with five odd cards, skipping the parity of five odds.
options.C: The sum is impossible, because five odd numbers have an odd sum and $30$ is even.
options.D: First pick any five odd cards, and say that choice is what creates the target total $30$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Xavier has a $5$ by $4$ rectangular grid of small squares. He wants to know whether the total number of small squares is even or odd without multiplying $5 \times 4$.

What can he decide?

options.A: Call the row count $5$ the parity answer, without using both dimensions.
options.B: Ignore that one side is even, and treat the parity as unknown until the product is formed.
options.C: The total is even, because at least one side length is even.
options.D: Say the even-or-odd decision is what creates the $5$ by $4$ grid sizes.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Qasim studies the expression $3n+4$ for whole-number values of $n$.

How should he classify its parity?

options.A: Call $3n+4$ a letter-number label only, without testing whether values stay even, stay odd, or change.
options.B: Say that calling the expression parity-changing is what creates the values of $3n+4$, instead of checking values of $n$.
options.C: It can be even or odd depending on $n$: for $n=1$ it is $7$ (odd), and for $n=2$ it is $10$ (even).
options.D: Decide from the printed coefficient $3$ alone, without testing any value of $n$.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Zaid wants an expression for the $n$th even number and the $n$th odd number by position.

Which pair is correct?

options.A: Call the answer even-odd labels only, without linking position $n$ to a formula.
options.B: Say that writing $2n$ and $2n-1$ is what creates the positions $1,2,3,\ldots$, instead of reading $n$ as position.
options.C: The $n$th even number is $2n$ and the $n$th odd number is $2n-1$ (for $n=1,2,3,\ldots$).
options.D: Use the same formulas to list every multiple of $3$, as if even/odd position rules settled that sequence too.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Ira draws a closed shape with three corner points P, Q and R joined by three straight sides.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: The shape is named only by one corner point, such as P.
options.B: The shape is a triangle even if one side is left open.
options.C: The shape is triangle PQR, with three sides and three angles at P, Q and R.
options.D: The shape is a triangle because the letter R is printed largest on the page.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Anya has drawn base AB of length 5 cm. She must build triangle ABC with AC = 5 cm and BC = 5 cm.

Where should she place point C?

options.A: Anywhere on a compass arc drawn from A alone, ignoring B.
options.B: At any point that is 5 cm from A, even if its distance from B is different.
options.C: At a meeting point of the arc centred at A with radius 5 cm and the arc centred at B with radius 5 cm.
options.D: At the printed midpoint mark on segment AB, because that mark is darkest.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Uday has three sticks of lengths 3 cm, 5 cm and 9 cm. He wants to know whether they can be the side lengths of a triangle.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: The answer is 9 cm, because that is the longest length.
options.B: Yes, because each length is a positive whole number.
options.C: No, because 3 + 5 = 8 is not greater than 9.
options.D: First construct the triangle with compass and ruler; only then decide whether the sides exist.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Isha has two sticks of lengths $4$ cm and $9$ cm. She wants a third stick so the three lengths can form a triangle.

Which claim about the third length $x$ is correct?

options.A: The answer is "fixed side lengths", naming that phrase instead of giving a range for $x$.
options.B: Any $x$ from $5$ cm to $13$ cm inclusive works, including the endpoints $5$ and $13$.
options.C: $x$ must satisfy $5 < x < 13$, because $|9-4| < x < 9+4$ with the endpoints excluded.
options.D: She must first construct the triangle with compass arcs, and only then decide which $x$ values are allowed.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Anya must construct a triangle given sides $AB=6$ cm, $AC=5$ cm, and the included angle at $A$ equal to $50^\circ$.

Which construction plan is correct?

options.A: Answer "base side", naming that phrase instead of placing the $50^\circ$ angle between the two given sides.
options.B: Say that drawing the finished triangle is what creates the given sides and included angle, instead of building from those data.
options.C: Draw $AB=6$ cm as a base, make a $50^\circ$ angle at $A$, mark $AC=5$ cm along the new arm, and join $C$ to $B$.
options.D: Copy the printed measure $50$ and treat that single number as the finished triangle, without using the two side lengths.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Deepak is given included side $BC = 5$ cm with $\angle B = 40^{\circ}$ and $\angle C = 60^{\circ}$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the answer base, without deciding whether the angle arms can meet to form a triangle.
options.B: Say that the meeting of the arms is what creates the given angles $40^{\circ}$ and $60^{\circ}$.
options.C: Draw $BC = 5$ cm; mark $40^{\circ}$ at $B$ and $60^{\circ}$ at $C$; the arms meet at $A$, and a triangle exists because $40^{\circ}+60^{\circ}<180^{\circ}$.
options.D: Decide only from the printed length $5$ cm, without using the two given angles.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Omkar walks at a steady speed of 3/4 km each hour. He walks for 2 hours at that same rate.

What total distance does he walk?
author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Esha has 24 beads. She wants 3/8 of them for a bracelet.

How many beads does she need?

options.A: 3 beads, reading only the numerator.
options.B: 8 beads, reading only the denominator.
options.C: 9 beads
options.D: 24 ÷ 3 × 8 beads

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Veena multiplies the fractions 2/3 and 3/4.

What product should she obtain?

options.A: 3/4, keeping only the second fraction.
options.B: 8/9, by dividing with reciprocals as if the task were fraction division.
options.C: 1/2, by taking two of the three equal parts of 3/4 (or (2×3)/(3×4)).
options.D: 2/3, because that fraction is printed first.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Mona shades a unit square. She takes $\frac{1}{2}$ of the square and then $\frac{1}{3}$ of that half to show $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{3}$.

Which reading of the shaded product is correct?

options.A: Call the rectangle area the product label, without linking it to the shaded fraction of the unit square.
options.B: Shade $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{3}$ even if the whole region is not the unit square.
options.C: The shaded piece is $\frac{1}{6}$ of the unit square, because one half of one third (or one third of one half) is one sixth.
options.D: Use the same shading story to find the perimeter of the unit square.

author: grok

subject: maths
stem:
Esha multiplies $\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{4}{5}$.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: Call the product "denominator", without multiplying numerators and denominators.
options.B: Multiply the numerators only, keeping one denominator unchanged.
options.C: $\frac{2 \times 4}{3 \times 5} = \frac{8}{15}$.
